# nb-studio build

## build ci configure

Configure a repository’s CI

For whoever manages the project; may run again at any time, each run connecting one application to one target (pull requests, a branch or a tag, deployed in an environment). Each way makes the repository’s API key (the `CI deploy` preset limited to its Apps, as the caller) or gives it a fresh secret, and writes it as the repository secret; a branch or tag’s App that exists and is not the repository’s yet is recorded for it, so the key reaches it. `direct` and `template` then commit the workflow file (a repository Studio created, once initialized) or propose it in a pull request (added to the one still open); `agent` gives the agent an issue to set the CI up, whose brief never holds the key. Neither the way nor the application is stored: only the pull request or the issue, until it is merged or finished. A failure after the run is checked is answered in the connection (`lastError`), not as an error.

```bash
nb-studio build ci configure <repo>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |

| Flag               | Type      | Description                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `--method`         | direct \\ | template \\                                                                                                                          | agent | `direct`: Studio writes the standard workflow of the application and target; `template`: Studio writes `workflowFiles` as given; `agent`: an issue asks `agentId` to set the CI up. Each needs the repository reached through a Git connection; the ways done by hand are sent nowhere. |
| `--app`            | json      | The application the run connects; one at the repository’s root, named after it, when left out. Used for this run only, never stored. |
| `--target`         | json      | What starts the CI and where it deploys; pull requests to the `preview` environment when left out.                                   |
| `--workflow-files` | json      | The one file `template` writes, valid YAML in `.github/workflows/`.                                                                  |
| `--agent-id`       | string    | The agent the issue of `agent` is given to.                                                                                          |
| `--file`           | path      | The request body as a JSON object; the flags override its fields.                                                                    |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `POST /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}/ci/configure` (`repositoryDeploymentsConfigureCi`)

**Examples:**

```bash
nb-studio build ci configure acme/shop --file run.json
```

## build ci connection

Read where a repository’s CI stands

For whoever sees the project: each App CI reported for the repository with its last build and upload (`apps`, connected only by its own reports), the outcome the last "Configure CI" run awaits (its pull request or agent’s issue), and the API key Studio keeps. A pull request merged or closed since, and an issue finished since, are noticed here.

```bash
nb-studio build ci connection <repo>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `GET /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}/ci/connection` (`repositoryDeploymentsGetCiConnection`)

## build ci environments

List the environments CI may deploy to

For whoever is signed in: every environment of release management, in its order, with whether it is protected (every deployment there, CI’s included, waits for an approver to approve its request). "Configure CI" offers them as the target’s environment. A bounded list, not paged.

```bash
nb-studio build ci environments
```

**Output:** A list (table columns: `id`, `name`, `protected`); with `--json`, `result.data` is the array and `result.meta` the paging.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `GET /api/repositoryDeployments/ciWorkflows/environments` (`repositoryDeploymentsListCiEnvironments`)

## build ci remove

Remove an App from a repository’s CI list

For whoever manages the project: takes an App (or, with `pullRequests=true`, an application’s pull request Apps) off the repository’s list in an environment. Its link to the repository goes and the CI key narrows to the Apps left; the builds reported until now stop counting for it, so CI’s next report brings it back. The App itself stays: deleting it is release management’s.

```bash
nb-studio build ci remove <repo> <app> --environment <string>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |
| `app`    | The App as listed; the application’s ID for its pull requests’ Apps.   |

| Flag              | Type    | Description                                                                                                    |
| ----------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--environment`   | string  | The environment the row is listed in. (required)                                                               |
| `--pull-requests` | boolean | `true` for the row of the application’s pull request Apps; `false` by default.                                 |
| `--yes`           | boolean | Go ahead without asking “Remove this App from the repository’s CI list? CI reporting it again brings it back.” |

**Output:** Nothing; prints `Done.`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `DELETE /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}/ci/apps/{appId}` (`repositoryDeploymentsRemoveCiApp`)

## build ci rotate

Rotate a repository’s CI key

For whoever manages the project: gives the API key Studio keeps for the repository’s CI a new secret and writes it as the repository secret at once. A failure is answered in the setup (`lastError`). With `reveal: true` (`--reveal`) the secret is answered once in `secret` instead, for a CI Studio cannot write to (another host, or CI that runs elsewhere): store it as `NB_STUDIO_API_KEY` yourself, such as `… --reveal --json | jq -er .result.data.secret | gh secret set NB_STUDIO_API_KEY -R owner/repo`. It needs no Git connection, is never shown again, and leaves the setup `manual`, which Studio does not rotate by itself; a failure is then an error.

```bash
nb-studio build ci rotate <repo>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |

| Flag       | Type    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--reveal` | boolean | Answer the secret once (`secret`) instead of writing it to the repository, for a CI Studio cannot write to (another host, or CI that runs elsewhere): store it as the CI secret `NB_STUDIO_API_KEY` yourself. Needs no Git connection. The setup becomes `manual`, so Studio no longer rotates the key by itself; it is never shown again, and revealing again gives a new secret. |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `POST /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}/ci/rotate` (`repositoryDeploymentsRotateCiKey`)

## build ci setup

Set a repository’s CI key up again

For whoever manages the project. Makes the repository’s API key (the `CI deploy` preset limited to its Apps, as the caller, who gives only what they hold; it may create the repository’s Apps, such as its pull requests’) again, or gives the existing one a new secret, and writes it as the repository secret; the workflows are left as the repository has them (`POST …/ci/configure` writes them). A failure is answered in the setup (`state: manual`, `lastError`), not as an error. With `reveal: true` (`--reveal`) the secret is answered once in `secret` instead, for a CI Studio cannot write to (another host, or CI that runs elsewhere): store it as `NB_STUDIO_API_KEY` yourself, such as `… --reveal --json | jq -er .result.data.secret | gh secret set NB_STUDIO_API_KEY -R owner/repo`. It needs no Git connection, is never shown again, and leaves the setup `manual`, which Studio does not rotate by itself; a failure is then an error.

```bash
nb-studio build ci setup <repo>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |

| Flag       | Type    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--reveal` | boolean | Answer the secret once (`secret`) instead of writing it to the repository, for a CI Studio cannot write to (another host, or CI that runs elsewhere): store it as the CI secret `NB_STUDIO_API_KEY` yourself. Needs no Git connection. The setup becomes `manual`, so Studio no longer rotates the key by itself; it is never shown again, and revealing again gives a new secret. |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `POST /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}/ci/setup` (`repositoryDeploymentsSetUpCi`)

**Examples:**

```bash
nb-studio build ci setup acme/shop
nb-studio build ci setup acme/shop --reveal --json | jq -er .result.data.secret | gh secret set NB_STUDIO_API_KEY -R acme/shop-ci
```

## build ci workflows

Generate the standard CI workflow of an application

For whoever is signed in: the workflow file of one application and target (`nb-studio-<app>-<purpose>.yml`: the App ID without its environment, then `preview` for pull requests or the environment’s name, such as `nb-studio-crm-preview.yml` or `nb-studio-crm-staging.yml`): pull requests that change the application’s directory each deployed to their own App, every push to a branch, or every tag matching a pattern, deployed in the target’s environment. It names no repository or commit: the CLI reads them from the CI run. Nothing is written.

```bash
nb-studio build ci workflows
```

| Flag               | Type    | Description                                                                                               |
| ------------------ | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--app`            | json    |                                                                                                           |
| `--target`         | json    | Pull requests to the `preview` environment when left out.                                                 |
| `--default-branch` | string  | The repository’s default branch, which a branch target builds when it names none; `main` when left out.   |
| `--managed`        | boolean | Whether Studio keeps the key (a run Studio carries out); otherwise the header says how to add it by hand. |
| `--file`           | path    | The request body as a JSON object; the flags override its fields.                                         |

**Output:** A list (table columns: `path`); with `--json`, `result.data` is the array and `result.meta` the paging.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `POST /api/repositoryDeployments/ciWorkflows/generate` (`repositoryDeploymentsGenerateCiWorkflows`)

**Examples:**

```bash
nb-studio build ci workflows --file run.json --json
```

## build repo set

Replace the Apps a repository builds

For whoever manages the project. `apps` is the complete set: an App left out is unlinked. Linking an App also asks for configuring it in release management. `plan`, the "Deploy & previews" choices, is applied on top of `apps`: Studio creates the Apps a staging or production environment needs, named after the repository (`<repo>`, `<repo>-staging`), as the caller, who must be allowed to create Apps or deploy to every App, and unlinks the role an environment left out. The preview choice changes nothing: previews are the repository’s CI’s, one App per pull request it deploys. CI also records the Apps it builds without this.

```bash
nb-studio build repo set <repo>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |

| Flag     | Type | Description                                                                                           |
| -------- | ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--apps` | json |                                                                                                       |
| `--plan` | json | The simple choices: the Apps they need are created and linked, and a role they leave out is unlinked. |
| `--file` | path | The request body as a JSON object; the flags override its fields.                                     |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `PUT /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}` (`repositoryDeploymentsReplaceRepositoryDeployment`)

**Examples:**

```bash
nb-studio build repo set acme/shop --file apps.json
```

## build status

Report where CI stands with a build

Optional, for showing a build’s progress: CI names the App, the commit and the repository (`owner/repo`; else the App’s, else its key’s), the CLI reading the last two from CI’s environment. A repository’s CI key naming another repository is refused (`REPOSITORY_MISMATCH`). It requires the `upload` action on the App, or the repository’s CI key for an App of the repository; an App not made yet (CI reports before `nb-studio app ensure`) takes the repository’s CI key or a credential that may create Apps. Studio verifies first that the commit belongs to the repository (an open pull request’s head, on the default branch, tagged, or another branch’s head) and shows the build on the App and, for a pull request’s head, on the issues it is linked to. CI’s scoped API key acts as a key.

```bash
nb-studio build status --app <string> --state <string>
```

| Flag           | Type      | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--app`        | string    | The App the build is of, which `nb-studio app ensure` makes; `<app>-pr-<number>` for a pull request’s preview by convention. (required)                                                                                                                     |
| `--sha`        | string    | The full commit hash the archive is built from; it must belong to the repository. (required; default from pull_request.head.sha of $GITHUB_EVENT_PATH or $GITHUB_SHA or $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_SHA or $CI_COMMIT_SHA)                              |
| `--repository` | string    | The repository the commit is verified in, as `owner/repo`; when none is named, the one the App was recorded or made for, else the one whose CI key the credential is. A CI key may name only its own. (default from $GITHUB_REPOSITORY or $CI_PROJECT_PATH) |
| `--state`      | queued \\ | building \\                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | failed \\ | succeeded | Where the build stands. (required) |
| `--logs`       | string    | The address of the build's log, such as the CI run.                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `--message`    | string    | One line about it, such as why it failed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key); needs the action `rel.apps/upload`.

**Request:** `POST /api/builds/report` (`buildsReportBuild`)

**Examples:**

```bash
nb-studio build status --app my-app-pr-12 --state building --logs <ci-run-url>
nb-studio build status --repository acme/my-app --app my-app-staging --sha <sha> --state failed
```

## build workflow

Generate the CI workflow building a repository’s Apps

For whoever sees the project: the GitHub Actions workflow CI starts from, building each pull request that touches the repository’s application into its own App in the `preview` environment and uploading each build to Studio. Other targets (a branch, a tag, another environment) come from "Configure CI" (`POST …/ci/configure`, `POST /api/repositoryDeployments/ciWorkflows/generate`).

```bash
nb-studio build workflow <repo>
```

| Argument | Description                                                            |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repo`   | The repository as `owner/repo`, among the projects the caller may see. |

**Output:** One record, field by field; with `--json`, `result.data`.

**Who:** People (a sign-in or an API key).

**Request:** `GET /api/repositoryDeployments/{resourceId}/ciWorkflow` (`repositoryDeploymentsGetCiWorkflow`)

**Examples:**

```bash
nb-studio build workflow acme/shop --json
```
